analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal financing for manufactured home communities on basic tenant protections like lease renewals and rent-increase notice.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote in the Senate and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: People in manufactured home communities usually own their home but rent the land under it, and they can face sudden rent hikes, eviction, or forced moves. This bill would make federal loan programs for buying or building these communities available only to owners who give residents a renewable one-year lease, 60-day written notice of rent increases (more notice for larger increases), a grace period on rent, the right to sell their home in place, and notice plus a chance to buy the community before it is sold. Owners who violate the rules would owe tenants money and could lose access to federal financing.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in manufactured home communities whose owners use HUD-insured or Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac financing. They would gain stable one-year leases, advance notice and written justification of rent increases, time to catch up on late rent, the right to sell their home without moving it, and compensation when owners break the rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufactured home residents who lease their lots

how_it_helps.text: Owners of communities financed through the covered federal loan programs would have to give tenants one-year leases that renew unless there is good cause for non-renewal.

Tenants would get at least 60 days' written notice of rent increases or new charges, with extra notice for increases above 5 percent, and a written justification tied to the community's actual operating costs.
Tenants would get a 5-day grace period on rent, a 15-day right to cure a default, and the right to sell their manufactured home in place rather than being forced to move it.
Before selling or closing a community, the owner would have to give 60 days' notice and negotiate in good faith with tenants who want to buy it.

Violations would carry penalties paid to tenants, such as repaying illegal rent increases with interest plus 25 percent, and repeat violators could be barred from federal housing financing for at least two years.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and investors who buy, build, or rehabilitate manufactured home communities with federally backed financing. They would have to include the protections in every lease they use, document compliance, and pay tenant compensation and potential exclusion from federal programs when they violate the rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Manufactured home community owners and investors

drawbacks.text: The protections only reach communities financed through the covered federal programs; owners who use other financing would face no new requirements, so many residents could remain unprotected.

Tying financing to tenant protections and penalties could make some lenders and park owners avoid these federal loan programs, which an honest supporter would acknowledge could reduce the pool of capital available to buy or improve communities.
Owners would bear documentation and compliance costs, including submitting standard lease agreements to regulators to prove the protections are in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents, the benefits are concrete and immediate: predictable leases, notice before rent hikes, and the ability to sell the home they own without moving it. The costs fall on community owners, and the main legitimate concern is that conditioning federal financing could push some deals to non-federal lenders, shrinking the bill's coverage rather than lowering overall protection. The protections also set only a floor, and state laws offering more would remain in force.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Shaheen introduced the bill on June 22, 2023, with Senators Blumenthal and Fetterman as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufactured home community owners and investors keep access to federal financing with no lease conditions or tenant penalties attached. Residents gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Manufactured Housing Tenant's Bill of Rights Act.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one ever had to go on record for or against it.

industries.industry: Manufactured home community owners and investors (including REITs and portfolio buyers)
industries.note: These owners profit from lot rents and from buying up communities; the bill would condition their access to federal financing on lease protections, rent-increase notice, tenant sale rights, and cash penalties for violations. Its value to residents comes directly out of the owner's flexibility to raise rents and resell communities.

industries.industry: Lenders and mortgage brokers in the manufactured housing community finance market
industries.note: Lenders making HUD-insured or enterprise-purchased community loans would face added borrower-certification and documentation requirements, and some loans might move to financing outside the covered programs. Lenders already making compliant loans would face little change.

The two mortgage companies would be barred from purchasing community loans without the tenant protections and would have to publish which properties are covered and develop a standard site lease. The new commission would include a representative from each company, giving them a seat in shaping future standards.
